item.title: Tax attorney: Investor interest growing in CNMI incentive programs
item.description: Tina Azarvand, managing partner of Azarvand Tax Law, said mainland investors are expressing growing interest in relocating businesses to the Northern Mariana Islands through the Commonwealth Economic Incentive Act and the Commonwealth Economic Development Authority's Qualifying Certificate program, though many are waiting to see how the newer incentive program is implemented. item.content:encoded:
Tina Azarvand, managing partner of Azarvand Tax Law, said mainland investors are expressing growing interest in relocating businesses to the Northern Mariana Islands through the Commonwealth Economic Incentive Act and the Commonwealth Economic Development Authority's Qualifying Certificate program, though many are waiting to see how the newer incentive program is implemented.

Azarvand said she has discussed CNMI investment opportunities with clients who initially sought information about Puerto Rico's tax incentives but became interested in exploring the commonwealth's programs.

"There is definitely interest in the CNMI," she said, noting that one prospective investor traveled from Florida to visit the islands and evaluate opportunities firsthand.

Among those expressing interest are two firms considering operations in the CNMI. One is involved in private equity with a broad range of investment interests, while the other focuses on service-based businesses that can operate remotely and export services outside the islands, she said.

Azarvand declined to identify the companies, saying discussions remain ongoing.

The firms initially viewed CEDA's QC program as their primary incentive option. The QC program provides qualifying businesses tax benefits in exchange for investments that support economic development in the CNMI.

They are now also evaluating opportunities under the economic incentive act, a recently enacted program aimed at attracting new investment and business relocation through additional tax-related benefits.

"They've kind of been wanting to see how this CEIA incentive program goes and see the viability for them as well," Azarvand said.

Azarvand said awareness of the CNMI's incentive programs remains limited among tax professionals on the mainland, including attorneys who specialize in Puerto Rico tax incentives.

"Most tax attorneys I speak with don't even know of the CNMI Qualifying Certificate program," she said.

She said that lack of awareness presents an opportunity for the CNMI to market its incentive programs more aggressively as officials seek to diversify the economy and attract new private-sector investment.

item.title: Federal judge rules against administration in American Samoa seabed mining lease

item.content:encoded:
A federal judge in Hawaii has ruled in favor of environmental groups opposing a seabed mining lease sale in American Samoa, finding that the National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act when it approved the sale.

The lease sale was set for Thursday, California time. The judge did not specifically issue an injunction canceling the sale, although the agency consultation was voided.

Faʻasao Amerika Samoa and Conservation Council for Hawaiʻi, represented by the environmental law organization Earthjustice, filed a lawsuit after the National Marine Fisheries Service determined that the Marine Minerals Administration lease sale was not likely to adversely affect endangered species.

The court ruled that the Fisheries Service accepted the administration’s definition of the “agency action” as the lease sale itself, not post-lease activity.

“By doing so, [National Marine Fisheries Service] only considered the preliminary effects of the lease sale and did not even attempt to consider potential effects of post-leasing activities. NMFS’s cramped, expedited, informal consultation is apparently unprecedented in the context of leasing on the [Outer Continental Shelf],” the ruling stated.

In a news release Wednesday, Earthjustice said the ruling was a win for the people of American Samoa, “as well as the whales, sharks, and sea turtles who call the waters surrounding these islands home.”

“It recognizes that the law requires the government to understand the full repercussions of its actions before letting this untested industry destroy one of the most pristine parts of the ocean on the planet,” said Chris Eaton, Earthjustice attorney.

Last year, the Trump administration vowed to fast-track seabed mining to give the United States access to critical minerals deep in the ocean.

A lease sale for up to 69 million acres east and west of the Mariana Islands is set for Dec. 16. The American Samoa and Mariana Islands leases involve areas within the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone.

On Tuesday morning, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration held a virtual public hearing on an application from a company that wants to look for polymetallic nodules in international waters.

Eco Minerals, previously known as Deep Sea Rare Minerals, wants to explore an area of seabed about 700 miles east-northeast of Guam, as well as eight areas in the Eastern Pacific’s Clarion-Clipperton Zone.

Those who testified in the hearing urged regulators to deny the license, arguing that the deep-sea ecosystem is not well understood and mining could cause long-term harm.

item.title: NWS urges vigilance as dry season begins across Guam and CNMI

A dry season-like pattern is expected to persist across the Marianas through the weekend, bringing mostly sunny skies, spotty showers and strengthening trade
item.content:encoded:
The National Weather Service is urging residents of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands to remain weather-aware as drought conditions develop across the region and El Niño keeps the potential for late-season tropical activity above normal.

A dry season-like pattern is expected to persist across the Marianas through the weekend, bringing mostly sunny skies, spotty showers and strengthening trade winds, according to the National Weather Service in Guam. Fire danger on Guam has risen to the high category as rainfall remains limited and vegetation continues to dry out.

Despite the dry conditions, Marcus Landon Aydlett, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Guam office, said residents should not overlook the threat of tropical cyclones.

"The risk for late-season tropical cyclones remains elevated through the end of the year and into early 2027 compared with other years," Aydlett said, citing the ongoing El Niño pattern.

No tropical cyclone development is expected during the next seven days, but forecasters said El Niño conditions could continue to influence weather across the western Pacific through the remainder of the year.

The weather service said a wetter pattern may develop later next week and continue into December, providing some relief to drought-affected areas across Micronesia. Residents with low or empty water catchments are encouraged to collect rainwater when showers occur.

item.title: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit
item.description: When the White House announced big improvements in the number of people dying from fatal drug overdoses earlier this week, officials pointed to hopeful new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showing U.S. drug deaths have plunged to their lowest level in roughly a decade, saving nearly 50,000 lives each year. item.content:encoded:
When the White House announced big improvements in the number of people dying from fatal drug overdoses earlier this week, officials pointed to hopeful new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showing U.S. drug deaths have plunged to their lowest level in roughly a decade, saving nearly 50,000 lives each year.

But leading drug policy researchers say the White House statement also made misleading claims about the timing and cause of the remarkable public health success when it said that gains occurred primarily over the last 18 months due to policies enacted under President Trump's leadership.

"The historic decline in drug overdose deaths demonstrates that America is unequivocally winning the fight against illicit drugs," White House Office of National Drug Control Policy director Sara Carter said in a statement .

Carter credited heightened border security under Trump and claims of success dismantling "narco-terrorist" organizations for the recovery. "Critically, this represents a an approximately 41.5% decrease in total drug overdose deaths compared to the peak under the previous administration," the statement said.

What the White House failed to disclose is that declines in overdose fatalities began much earlier, under the Biden administration, with most of the gains occurring before Trump returned to office.

"Since the spring of 2023, we have seen a steady decline in overdose deaths," said Vanda Felbab-Brown, a drug policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "The fact that it has been sustained is very important."

According to CDC data, reductions in drug deaths began in 2023 and have continued steadily for at least 39 consecutive months — not 18 months as the ONDCP statement said. By the time Biden left office, fatal overdoses had already dropped by roughly one-third, an improvement described by addiction experts at the time as unprecedented.

Nabarun Dasgupta, a street drug researcher at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, was one of the first scientists to detect the stunning drop in overdose deaths. He said the trend toward fewer deaths began in some regions and among some demographic groups as early as 2021 and rapidly gained momentum nationwide.

"It was really the period early 2024 through spring 2025 where we were seeing the greatest rate of decline that we've ever seen," Dasgupta said.

Deaths from fentanyl smuggled into the U.S. from Mexico first began to rise in 2013 during President Obama's time in office and accelerated during Trump's first term. Fentanyl overdoses spiked sharply the first two years of Biden's presidency, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite progress, fentanyl remains the leading cause of drug deaths nationwide.

Dasgupta, Felbab-Brown and other and addiction experts credit the Biden administration for rolling out policy responses that included wider access to healthcare, making the opioid overdose medication naloxone more readily available, and negotiating a deal with China that disrupted the flow of industrial chemicals used to make fentanyl.

The Biden team also scored significant drug interdiction wins against the Mexican cartels that smuggle fentanyl. "We have certainly been seeing over many years, going back to the Biden administration, important efforts to crack down against them," said Felbab-Brown.

Dasgupta and Felbab-Brown both said improvements in reducing drug mortality have continued under Trump. They said it's important to have an accurate timeline of the overdose crisis because researchers are still trying to understand why deaths involving fentanyl surged and why so many fewer people are now dying.

NPR asked the White House about progress in the fentanyl fight under Biden. In an emailed statement, ONDCP director Carter, a former podcaster, journalist and Fox News contributor , blamed Biden for failing to secure the U.S.-Mexico border and for allowing drug deaths to surge in the first place.

"While drug overdose deaths eventually began to decline following the peak, the Biden Administration doesn't get to take credit for overseeing the highest drug overdose numbers in history, then bringing them down from their own failure," Carter said.

Responding to CDC data showing drug deaths began to plummet much earlier than stated the White House announcement, Carter said "this could be misinterpreted as progress on a graph, but it was not progress."

According to Carter, the Trump administration is now well-positioned to build on overdose death reductions made over the last three years, in part by maintaining border security and by continuing to "relentlessly attack" drug gangs.

"We are dismantling and eliminating the violent cartels and drug trafficking organizations through coordinated operations," she said.

But Felbab-Brown at Brookings said she doesn't share the Trump administration's confidence that there has been significant progress "dismantling and eliminating" narco-terrorist organizations.

"I cannot think of one narco-terrorist organization that has been dismantled," she said. "They all continue operating and they are all very strong. They all continue smuggling drugs."

Military experts have also questioned the effectiveness, and legality , of Trump's ongoing strikes against civilian boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, described as smuggling vessels by the Pentagon.

Dasgupta, the addiction researcher at UNC, said he's also concerned about whether progress reducing drug deaths can be sustained next year as the Trump administration implements deep cuts to Medicaid passed by the Republican Congress.

The Congressional Budget Office has estimated the cuts could mean as many as 10 million Americans losing access to health insurance coverage.

"Medicaid is the largest funder of addiction services in the United States," Dasgupta said. "Cutting Medicaid eligibility or making it harder to access forms of effective addiction treatment is guaranteed to leave people out in the cold."

item.title: 'I Play Rocky' and 'Elsinore' can't land their punches, even with star performances
item.description: It's not rare at this time of year to hear Oscar buzz for actors playing real-life people, like Timothée Chalamet as Bob Dylan , to name a recent example. item.content:encoded:
It's not rare at this time of year to hear Oscar buzz for actors playing real-life people, like Timothée Chalamet as Bob Dylan , to name a recent example. It's less common to have two biographical films, Elsinore and I Play Rocky , in which the Oscars themselves factor into the story.

In Elsinore , set in London in 1989, Andrew Scott plays the actor Ian Charleson, who's best known for co-starring in the Best Picture-winning Chariots of Fire . It's a frustrating kind of fame; Ian can't even get into a cab without the driver humming Vangelis ' memorable theme music.

But Ian has much more to worry about: He's a gay man living with AIDS at a time when the diagnosis is a death sentence. Soon, though, a rare career opportunity presents itself. Daniel Day-Lewis has just dropped out of Hamlet at the National Theatre, and the production needs a new prince of Denmark.

Ian, who loves the play deeply, lands the role. He's determined to make it work, despite the warnings of his doctor, Margaret Johnson — a trailblazer in HIV and AIDS treatment, played by a terrifically stern Olivia Colman. Dr. Johnson knows that rehearsals and performances will take a toll on his already poor health.

One of Ian's harshest critics is the pioneering queer director Derek Jarman, played by David Dawson, who criticizes him for not going public with his sexuality. It's poignant and meaningful, then, that Charleson is played by an openly gay actor, especially one as good as Scott, who didn't get the attention he deserved for his delicate, haunting work in the 2023 drama All of Us Strangers .

In Elsinore , Scott gives a moving, if more conspicuously effortful, performance: He has to declaim lines from Shakespeare's greatest play and slowly succumb to terminal illness. Scott is much better than the movie, which, as directed by the Australian filmmaker Simon Stone and written by Stephen Beresford, often plays like a feature-length trailer for itself. Too much of it unfolds in montages that mash Ian's art and his illness clumsily together, ultimately sapping both of meaning.

Elsinore is a tearjerker that memorializes an actor's final role. I Play Rocky , directed by Peter Farrelly from a script by Peter Gamble, is a crowd-pleaser that celebrates a legendary arrival. As it begins, the young Sly Stallone — played by an excellent Anthony Ippolito — is a broke New York City nobody, eager to prove himself as an actor and screenwriter.

The movie takes us through Sly's early ups and downs. He's nearly evicted, adopts a stray dog, appears in a softcore-porn movie to pay some bills and puts up with his discouraging dad — an almost unrecognizable Matt Dillon . Sly gets more support from his girlfriend and soon wife, Sasha, who moves with him out to L.A. She's played by AnnaSophia Robb, doing what she can to liven up a straightforward loyal-spouse role.

Stallone famously wrote the script for Rocky in three-and-a-half days, inspired by a 1975 boxing match between Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner . I Play Rocky glosses over that and other story beats without providing much insight into Sly's creative process.

The drama kicks in, though, when the finished script draws interest from the film company United Artists, but Sly refuses to let them have Rocky unless he plays the lead. The ensuing negotiations are pretty entertaining to watch. P.J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell make a deft comic duo as the producers Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff, savvy industry gatekeepers who eventually come to believe in Sly as passionately as he believes in himself. And Tracy Letts is hilarious as a UA executive who wants a more bankable star, like Robert Redford or Burt Reynolds .

History, of course, will prove him dramatically wrong; Rocky will bring audiences to their feet, become the top-grossing film of 1976 and win the Oscar for Best Picture. But I Play Rocky seems to know this odds-defying outcome at every step. It's an underdog story in which the underdog's triumph feels preordained, a by-the-numbers movie in which the numbers are admittedly irresistible, like the enduring image of Stallone running up the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art. It does have a major asset in Ippolito, who's such a dead ringer for young Stallone that you can't help but believe in him, even when the movie around him doesn't go anywhere near the distance.

item.title: Got a canceled flight? 7 clever ways to get rebooked fast
item.description: A version of this story was originally published on June 17, 2025. This year, nearly 6 million travelers are projected to take domestic flights for the Thanksgiving holiday, according to an AAA forecast published in November .
item.content:encoded:
A version of this story was originally published on June 17, 2025.

This year, nearly 6 million travelers are projected to take domestic flights for the Thanksgiving holiday, according to an AAA forecast published in November .

If you plan on being one of those travelers in the coming days, make sure you know what to do in case your flight suddenly gets delayed or canceled.

Air travel has gotten notably worse over the past decade. In 2025, cancellations and delays surged, creating the worst on-time performance for airlines in the United States since 2014, according to a 2026 report by the U.S. PIRG Education Fund, a consumer advocacy group.

So, with holiday schlepping season kicking off this week, what's a weary traveler to do? Ahead, travel experts explain how to make rebooking flights less painful. Because what's worse than a canceled holiday flight is missing the holiday altogether.

Most people react to a cancellation by heading straight to the nearest customer service desk and queuing up to rebook their flight. The problem with that approach? Everyone else on your flight is doing that too.

"You have 300 people getting off the plane. There's maybe one, two people trying to help everyone. That clearly is the least efficient way," says travel reporter Chris Dong.

While standing in line, open up the airline app and rebook yourself, he says. There's often a seamless way to get it done, no customer service conversation necessary. During the holiday rush, when hundreds of other passengers may be trying to rebook at the same time, getting a head start on the airline's app can make an especially big difference.

If you have a travel credit card that gives you lounge access, head there to get one-on-one customer service. "Lounge agents are much more inclined to help you and are usually not as short-staffed," Dong says. "That can get you help quickly."

If you don't already have lounge access, see if you can purchase a day pass on-site. It may be well worth it depending on your flight cost and timeline.

All ticket holders are entitled to a refund if the airline cancels their flight and they don't accept whatever the airline is offering, such as a later flight and/or travel vouchers or vouchers for hotels or meals. However, most airlines in the U.S. aren't required to compensate you for delays or cancellations unless it's the airline's fault (think maintenance issues or staffing problems).

To find out what you're entitled to, check the Department of Transportation's Airline Cancellation and Delay Dashboard . Many major airlines have committed to giving passengers cost-free rebooking, meal vouchers, hotel accommodations, hotel transportation and more.

Once you know what your airline offers, say, a hotel, you can rest easy about what to do that night — and focus on rebooking for the next day.

Once you know what your airline will cover, check what your travel insurance will cover. Many credit cards include some travel insurance coverage, which can provide everything from trip cancellation to luggage insurance to any medical needs that might arise en route.

If you have flight time options when rebooking or flexibility in your travel schedule, choose the early-morning flight. They're your best bet to avoid delays or cancellations, Dong says.

If you're on the first flight out, there's little chance you'll have to wait for that aircraft coming in from another city because it's likely been sitting at the airport overnight.

This is especially worth considering during the holidays, when a single disruption can have a domino effect on subsequent flights. An early departure gives you more opportunities to get rebooked on another flight that same day if something goes wrong — because nobody wants to miss that family Thanksgiving dinner!

If the airline significantly delayed, significantly changed (see DOT website for details) or cancelled the flight and you originally booked your ticket directly with your airline, getting your money back should be no problem, even if the ticket is nonrefundable. But if you booked through a third party such as a travel agent or travel website, you'll have to go through them.

Remember that customer service representatives are likely dealing with hundreds of frustrated passengers during the holiday rush. Being patient and polite won't guarantee an exception, but it certainly won't hurt your chances, suggests Eulanda Osagiede , director of operations at Black Travel Alliance and chief operations officer at Black Travel Summit.

The best approach, she says, is to be "very nice, very friendly" with the customer service representative on the phone. So don't start yelling at them. Treating reps like the human beings they are can make all the difference.

When you're traveling for Thanksgiving, Hanukkah or Christmas, a delay doesn't just mean missing a few hours of vacation. It could mean missing the big family gathering or a favorite kiddo's holiday performance.

So before you leave, take a few minutes to research alternative routes to your destination. Are there other airports nearby? Could you drive part of the way? Are there trains or buses that could get you there if your flight falls through?

It's also worth saving your airline's customer service number, downloading its app, and keeping your confirmation numbers somewhere accessible offline. If you're traveling with kids, pack enough snacks, medications, entertainment and other essentials to get through an unexpected overnight stay.

You can't plan for every possible disruption, but you can make sure you're not starting from scratch when one happens.

This story was edited by Malaka Gharib. The visual editor is CJ Riculan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.

Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify , and sign up for our newsletter . Follow us on Instagram: @nprlifekit .

item.title: Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House
item.description: Updated November 19, 2026 at 4:03 AM ChST House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been nominated by House Democrats to serve as Speaker of the House when the party retakes the majority in the new year.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 19, 2026 at 4:03 AM ChST

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been nominated by House Democrats to serve as Speaker of the House when the party retakes the majority in the new year.

Wednesday's vote by House Democrats kickstarts the formal selection process for Speaker, which will take place at the start of the new Congress on January 3 with a vote on the floor of the House. If successful, as is widely expected, Jeffries will make history as the first Black lawmaker to serve in the job.

"Our message to the American people who are struggling in this failed economy is a simple one. We hear you, we see you, we feel you, and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you," Jeffries said after the vote.

Jeffries centered his remarks on cost of living issues, saying Democrats would fight to lower the cost of groceries, gas, housing and health care. And in the face of what he described as "unprecedented corruption," Jeffries said Democrats would work to hold officials accountable.

"Not for partisan reasons but for patriotic ones, because the American people deserve better," he said.

The New York Democrat ran uncontested, winning a closed-door vote by a tally of 251 to 11. His victory comes just over a week after House Republicans selected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio to be the conference's minority leader; in the Senate, Republicans tapped South Dakota's John Thune for a second term as party leader.

Jeffries, who's led House Democrats since 2023, will need just a simple majority of member votes in a Congress where Democrats are poised to control at least 257 seats, with several remaining races still to be decided.

It's a vastly different reality from what awaited House Republicans four years ago when they regained the House majority. Facing extremely narrow margins, GOP leaders struggled to unite the conference around a speaker and were forced to negotiate with a handful of far-right party holdouts in order to reach consensus. After multiple candidates failed to secure a majority, the party ultimately coalesced around the now outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.

While Jeffries will still have to navigate intraparty divides, the size of Democrats' majority affords him room to weather some dissent.

He's faced resistance from some within the party's left-most flank, who argue Democrats should prioritize advancing a more progressive agenda next year, lobbying for votes on Medicare for All and legislation that would stop the transfer of offensive weapons to Israel.

Among those who voted against Jeffries were a number of newly-elected members — some who won with the backing of the Democratic Socialists of America. In a statement after the vote, they said they have engaged in "good-faith conversations" with Jeffries to secure commitments on their policy priorities.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no."

Among those who signed the statement were members-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, both from New York; New Jersey's Adam Hamawy; Frederick Haynes of Texas; Colorado's Melat Kiros; Donavan McKinney of Michigan and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.

After the vote, Jeffries told reporters "the results of today's election speak for themselves."

"We're going to work hard throughout every corner of the caucus to deliver for the American people. Our job is to fight MAGA extremism — not each other — to fight MAGA extremism and to get big things done for the American people."

Given that Democrats will hold double digit margins in the chamber — an edge propelled by the success of more moderate candidates in districts President Trump carried in 2024 — it's unclear how much leverage the left wing of the party will have in the speaker's vote.

Divides inside the party may prove more pronounced in the Senate, where some Democrats are more publicly questioning whether current Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York is best suited to deliver on voter demands for change.

Schumer faces a challenge from Maryland's Chris Van Hollen, who announced his candidacy last week and is pitching himself as an alternative to the status quo, echoing much of the progressive populist messaging that several successful Senate candidates ran on this cycle. Like Schumer, Van Hollen has also served in Congress for decades.

Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate for nearly a decade, contends that he still has the needed votes to be elected majority leader. However, Van Hollen's challenge comes as a handful of current and incoming members have declined to back Schumer for the job.

Both sides still have time to shore up votes, with leadership elections set for early December.
